title: Arakhin 5
description: When consecrating one limb spreads to the whole animal, three dilemmas about vows for the altar left standing, a child under a month old and a utensil “valuated” on the principle that no one speaks for naught, and Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda on whether a gentile can valuate or be valuated.
topics: 🐂 “The leg of this animal is a burnt offering”: Rabbi Meir against Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon
⚖️ Inherent sanctity or sanctity of value, one limb or the whole animal, unblemished or blemished
❓ Three dilemmas left standing: the value of my head, my valuation and an ancestral field, each pledged for the altar
👶 A child under a month old: the Torah sets no valuation, but he can be the object of a vow
🗣️ “A person does not utter his words for naught”: the valuation of a utensil and of another’s animal
🌍 A gentile: valuated but does not valuate, or valuates but is not valuated?
🏗️ “You have nothing to do with us to build a house to our God” (Ezra 4:3), and what it means for Rabbi Yehuda

a1.he: ״רַגְלָהּ שֶׁל זוֹ עוֹלָה״ — יָכוֹל תְּהֵא כּוּלָּהּ עוֹלָה? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר ״כֹּל אֲשֶׁר יִתֵּן מִמֶּנּוּ לַה׳ יִהְיֶה קֹּדֶשׁ״ — מִמֶּנּוּ קוֹדֶשׁ וְלֹא כּוּלָּהּ קוֹדֶשׁ.

a2.he: יָכוֹל תֵּצֵא לְחוּלִּין? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: ״יִהְיֶה״ — בַּהֲוָיָיתָהּ תְּהֵא. הָא כֵּיצַד? תִּמָּכֵר לְצוֹרְכֵי עוֹלוֹת, וְדָמֶיהָ חוּלִּין, חוּץ מִדְּמֵי אוֹתוֹ אֵבֶר שֶׁבָּהּ, דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי מֵאִיר.

a3.he: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה וְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי וְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמְרִים: מִנַּיִן לָאוֹמֵר ״רַגְלָהּ שֶׁל זוֹ עוֹלָה״, שֶׁכּוּלָּהּ עוֹלָה? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: ״כֹּל אֲשֶׁר יִתֵּן מִמֶּנּוּ לַה׳ יִהְיֶה קֹּדֶשׁ״, לְרַבּוֹת אֶת כּוּלָּהּ.

a4.he: וַאֲפִילּוּ לְמַאן דְּאָמַר אֵין כּוּלָּהּ עוֹלָה, הָנֵי מִילֵּי דְּאַקְדֵּישׁ דָּבָר שֶׁאֵין הַנְּשָׁמָה תְּלוּיָה בּוֹ, אֲבָל דָּבָר שֶׁהַנְּשָׁמָה תְּלוּיָה בּוֹ — קָדְשָׁה כּוּלָּהּ.

a5.he: אֶלָּא, לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא בִּקְדוּשַּׁת הַגּוּף, הָא בִּקְדוּשַּׁת דָּמִים.

a6.he: וְהָא מָר הוּא דְּאָמַר: מַקְדִּישׁ זָכָר לְדָמָיו — קָדוֹשׁ קְדוּשַּׁת הַגּוּף!

a7.he: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא דְּאַקְדֵּישׁ כּוּלָּהּ, הָא דְּאַקְדֵּישׁ חַד אֵבֶר.

a8.he: חַד אֵבֶר נָמֵי אִיבְּעוֹיֵי אִיבַּעְיָא לַן, דְּבָעֵי רַבָּה: הִקְדִּישׁ אֵבֶר לְדָמָיו, מַהוּ?

a9.he: כִּי אִיבְּעִי לַן בְּתָם, הָכָא בְּבַעַל מוּם, דּוּמְיָא דַּחֲמוֹר.

a10.he: בַּעַל מוּם נָמֵי אִיבְּעוֹיֵי אִיבַּעְיָא לַן, דְּבָעֵי רַבָּה: ״דְּמֵי רֹאשִׁי לְגַבֵּי מִזְבֵּחַ״ מַהוּ? כִּי אִבַּעְיָא לָן מִקַּמֵּי דְּאֶשְׁמְעַהּ לְהָא מַתְנִיתָא, הַשְׁתָּא דְּשַׁמְעַהּ הָא מַתְנִיתָא — לָא מִיבַּעְיָא לַן.

a11.he: גּוּפָא, בָּעֵי רַבָּה: ״דְּמֵי רֹאשִׁי לְגַבֵּי מִזְבֵּחַ״ מַהוּ? נִידּוֹן בִּכְבוֹדוֹ, אוֹ אֵינוֹ נִידּוֹן בִּכְבוֹדוֹ?

a12.he: לָא אַשְׁכְּחַן בְּדָמִים דְּאֵינוֹ נִידּוֹן בִּכְבוֹדוֹ, אוֹ דִלְמָא לָא אַשְׁכְּחַן לְגַבֵּי מִזְבֵּחַ דְּנִידּוֹן בִּכְבוֹדוֹ? תֵּיקוּ.

a13.he: בָּעֵי רָבָא: ״עֶרְכִּי עָלַי לְגַבֵּי מִזְבֵּחַ״ מַהוּ? נִידּוֹן בְּהֶשֵּׂג יָד, אוֹ אֵין נִידּוֹן בְּהֶשֵּׂג יָד?

a14.he: לָא אַשְׁכְּחַן בַּעֲרָכִין דְּאֵין נִידּוֹן בְּהֶשֵּׂג יָד, אוֹ דִלְמָא לָא אַשְׁכְּחַן לְגַבֵּי מִזְבֵּחַ דְּמִיפְּרִיק אֶלָּא בְּשׇׁוְיוֹ? תֵּיקוּ.

a15.he: בָּעֵי רַב אָשֵׁי: הִקְדִּישׁ שְׂדֵה אֲחוּזָּה לְגַבֵּי מִזְבֵּחַ, מַהוּ? מִי אָמְרִינַן: לָא אַשְׁכְּחַן שְׂדֵה אֲחוּזָּה דְּמִיפָּרְקָא אֶלָּא ״בֵּית זֶרַע חוֹמֶר שְׂעוֹרִים בַּחֲמִשִּׁים שֶׁקֶל כָּסֶף״, אוֹ דִלְמָא לָא אַשְׁכְּחַן לְגַבֵּי מִזְבֵּחַ דְּמִיפְּרִיק אֶלָּא בְּשׇׁוְיוֹ? תֵּיקוּ.

a16.he: מַתְנִי׳ פָּחוֹת מִבֶּן חֹדֶשׁ נִידָּר, אֲבָל לֹא נֶעֱרָךְ.

a17.he: גְּמָ׳ תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הַמַּעֲרִיךְ פָּחוֹת מִבֶּן חֹדֶשׁ, רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר: נוֹתֵן דָּמָיו, וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים: לֹא אָמַר כְּלוּם.

a18.he: בְּמַאי קָמִיפַּלְגִי? רַבִּי מֵאִיר סָבַר: אֵין אָדָם מוֹצִיא דְּבָרָיו לְבַטָּלָה, יוֹדֵעַ שֶׁאֵין עֲרָכִין לְפָחוֹת מִבֶּן חֹדֶשׁ, וְגָמַר וְאָמַר לְשֵׁם דָּמִים; וְרַבָּנַן סָבְרִי: אָדָם מוֹצִיא דְּבָרָיו לְבַטָּלָה.

a19.he: כְּמַאן אָזְלָא הָא דְּאָמַר רַב גִּידֵּל אָמַר רַב: הָאוֹמֵר ״עֵרֶךְ כְּלִי עָלַי״ נוֹתֵן דָּמִים — כְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר. פְּשִׁיטָא דִּכְרַבִּי מֵאִיר אַתְיָא!

a20.he: מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא, אֲפִילּוּ כְּרַבָּנַן, הָתָם הוּא דְּטָעֵי, סָבַר: כִּי הֵיכִי דְּאִיכָּא עֲרָכִין לְבֶן חוֹדֶשׁ, אִיכָּא נָמֵי לְפָחוֹת מִבֶּן חוֹדֶשׁ.

a21.he: אֲבָל הָכָא דְּלֵיכָּא לְמִיטְעֵי, וַדַּאי אָדָם יוֹדֵעַ שֶׁאֵין עֵרֶךְ לִכְלִי, וְגָמַר וְאָמַר לְשֵׁם דָּמִים, קָמַשְׁמַע לַן.

b2.he: מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא: טַעְמָא דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר הָתָם, דְּגָזַר פָּחוֹת מִבֶּן חוֹדֶשׁ אַטּוּ בֶּן חוֹדֶשׁ, אֲבָל הָכָא דְּלֵיכָּא לְמִיגְזַר — אֵימָא לָא. קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן: טַעְמָא דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר דְּאֵין אָדָם מוֹצִיא דְּבָרָיו לְבַטָּלָה, לָא שְׁנָא הָכָא וְלָא שְׁנָא הָכָא.

b3.he: כְּמַאן אָזְלָא הָא דְּאָמַר רַבָּה בַּר יוֹסֵף אָמַר רַב, וְאָמְרִי לַהּ אָמַר רַב יֵיבָא בַּר יוֹסֵי אָמַר רַב: הַמַּקְדִּישׁ בֶּהֱמַת חֲבֵירוֹ נוֹתֵן דָּמֶיהָ? כְּמַאן — כְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר.

b4.he: הָא אַמְרַהּ רַב חֲדָא זִימְנָא, דְּאָמַר רַב גִּידֵּל אָמַר רַב: הָאוֹמֵר ״עֵרֶךְ כְּלִי עָלַי״ נוֹתֵן דָּמָיו! מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא הָתָם הוּא דְּיוֹדֵעַ שֶׁאֵין עֵרֶךְ לִכְלִי, וְגָמַר וְאָמַר לְשֵׁם דָּמִים.

b5.he: אֲבָל בְּהֵמָה, דְּבַת מִיקְדַּשׁ הִיא, אִיכָּא לְמֵימַר דְּהָכִי קָאָמַר: אִי אָמֵינָא לֵהּ לְמַרַּהּ מְזַבֵּין לַהּ נִיהֲלִי, תִּיקְדּוֹשׁ לַהּ מֵהַשְׁתָּא וְאַקְרְבַהּ, אֲבָל דְּמֵי לָא קָאָמַר, קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן.

b6.he: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: וְהוּא דְּאָמַר ״עָלַי״, אֲבָל אָמַר ״הֲרֵי זוֹ״ — לֹא.

b7.he: מַתְנִי׳ נָכְרִי — רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר: נֶעֱרָךְ, אֲבָל לֹא מַעֲרִיךְ. רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: מַעֲרִיךְ, אֲבָל לֹא נֶעֱרָךְ. וְזֶה וָזֶה מוֹדִים שֶׁנּוֹדְרִין וְנִידָּרִין.

b8.he: גְּמָ׳ תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מַעֲרִיכִין וְאֵין הַגּוֹיִם מַעֲרִיכִין.

b9.he: יָכוֹל לֹא יְהוּ נֶעֱרָכִין? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: ״אִישׁ״, דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי מֵאִיר.

b10.he: אָמַר רַבִּי מֵאִיר: וְכִי מֵאַחַר שֶׁמִּקְרָא אֶחָד מְרַבֶּה וּמִקְרָא אֶחָד מְמַעֵט, מִפְּנֵי מָה אֲנִי אוֹמֵר נֶעֱרָךְ וְלֹא מַעֲרִיךְ?

b11.he: מִפְּנֵי שֶׁרִיבָּה הַכָּתוּב בַּנֶּעֱרָכִין יוֹתֵר מִבַּמַּעֲרִיכִין, שֶׁהֲרֵי חֵרֵשׁ שׁוֹטֶה וְקָטָן נֶעֱרָךְ, אֲבָל לֹא מַעֲרִיכִין.

b12.he: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל נֶעֱרָכִין וְאֵין הַגּוֹיִם נֶעֱרָכִין; יָכוֹל לֹא יְהוּ מַעֲרִיכִין? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר ״אִישׁ״.

b13.he: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה: וְכִי מֵאַחַר שֶׁמִּקְרָא אֶחָד מְרַבֶּה וּמִקְרָא אֶחָד מְמַעֵט, מִפְּנֵי מָה אֲנִי אוֹמֵר נָכְרִי מַעֲרִיךְ וְלֹא נֶעֱרָךְ? מִפְּנֵי שֶׁרִיבָּה הַכָּתוּב בַּמַּעֲרִיכִין יוֹתֵר מִבַּנֶּעְרָכִין, שֶׁהֲרֵי טוּמְטוּם וְאַנְדְּרוֹגִינוֹס מַעֲרִיכִין אֲבָל לֹא נֶעֱרָכִין.

b14.he: אָמַר רָבָא: הִלְכְתֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר מִסְתַּבְּרָא, טַעְמֵיהּ לָא מִסְתַּבְּרָא, טַעְמָא דְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה מִסְתַּבְּרָא, הִלְכְתֵיהּ לָא מִסְתַּבְּרָא.

b15.he: הִלְכְתֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר מִסְתַּבְּרָא, דִּכְתִיב: ״לֹא לָכֶם וָלָנוּ לִבְנוֹת אֶת בֵּית אֱלֹהֵינוּ״, טַעְמֵיהּ לָא מִסְתַּבְּרָא, דְּקָא מַיְיתֵי לֵיהּ מֵחֵרֵשׁ שׁוֹטֶה וְקָטָן, שָׁאנֵי חֵרֵשׁ שׁוֹטֶה וְקָטָן דְּלָאו בְּנֵי דֵעָה נִינְהוּ.

b16.he: טַעְמָא דְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה מִסְתַּבְּרָא, דְּקָא מַיְיתֵי לֵיהּ מִטּוּמְטוּם וְאַנְדְּרוֹגִינוֹס, דְּאַף עַל גַּב דִּבְנֵי דֵעָה נִינְהוּ מַעֲטִינְהוּ רַחֲמָנָא. הִלְכְתֵיהּ לָא מִסְתַּבְּרָא, דִּכְתִיב: ״לֹא לָכֶם וָלָנוּ לִבְנוֹת אֶת בֵּית אֱלֹהֵינוּ״.

b17.he: וְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה, הַאי ״לָא לָכֶם וְלָנוּ״ מַאי עָבֵיד לֵיהּ? אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר אֲבִימִי: וְעֶרְכּוֹ נִגְנָז.

b18.he: אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה, לֹא יִמְעֲלוּ בּוֹ, דִּתְנַן: חָמֵשׁ חַטָּאוֹת הַמֵּתוֹת, וּמָעוֹת הַהוֹלְכוֹת לְיָם הַמֶּלַח — לֹא נֶהֱנִין וְלֹא מוֹעֲלִין!

b19.he: אַלְּמָה תַּנְיָא גַּבֵּי קׇדְשֵׁי גוֹיִם: בַּמֶּה דְּבָרִים אֲמוּרִים — בְּקׇדְשֵׁי מִזְבֵּחַ, אֲבָל בְּקׇדְשֵׁי בֶּדֶק הַבַּיִת מוֹעֲלִין בָּהֶן?!

b20.he: אֶלָּא אָמַר רָבָא: מִשּׁוּם רִפְיוֹן יָדַיִם הוּא, דִּכְתִיב: ״וַיְהִי עַם הָאָרֶץ מְרַפִּין יְדֵי עַם יְהוּדָה וּמְבַהֲלִים אוֹתָם לִבְנוֹת״.

messages.text: 5a

Continued from 4b: the Gemara asked why, if the baraita about the head of a cow deals with items consecrated for the altar, the sanctity does not spread through the whole cow, and it cites a baraita about one who says:

“The leg of this animal is a burnt offering,” one might have thought that all of the animal will be a burnt offering. Therefore, the verse states: “And if it is an animal of those that they bring as an offering to the Lord, anything of it that one gives to the Lord, it shall be sacred.” The verse indicates that the part of it that one gives will be sacred, but not all of the animal will be sacred.
messages.lead: In a case where one says:

verse.he: וְאִם־בְּהֵמָה אֲשֶׁר יַקְרִיבוּ מִמֶּנָּה קׇרְבָּן לַיהֹוָה כֹּל אֲשֶׁר יִתֵּן מִמֶּנּוּ לַיהֹוָה יִהְיֶה־קֹּדֶשׁ׃
verse.en: If [the vow concerns] any animal that may be brought as an offering to GOD, any such that may be given to GOD shall be holy.

messages.text: A non-sacred animal with a consecrated limb may not be sacrificed. Accordingly, one might have thought that the consecrated limb may be redeemed and thereby transferred to non-sacred status. Therefore the verse states: “Shall be,” meaning: It shall be as it is, i.e., the limb remains consecrated.

notes.he: שאר הבהמה לחולין:
notes.en: Might it go out: the rest of the animal, to non-sacred status.

notes.he: בקדושתה תהא:
notes.en: It shall be as it is: it shall remain in its sanctity.

messages.text: How is this possible, i.e., what should one do in this case? The animal should be sold for the needs of burnt offerings, i.e., to an individual who will sacrifice the entire animal as a burnt offering, and the payment received for the animal will be non-sacred, except for the payment received in exchange for that limb of it that was consecrated. This is the statement of Rabbi Meir.

notes.he: דהא לא אקדיש גופה:
notes.en: It is sold for the needs of a burnt offering, and its payment is non-sacred: since he did not consecrate the animal itself.

notes.he: שלא יקבל דמה כיון דנחתא ליה קדושת הגוף אינו רשאי למוכרה ואם מכרה אינה מכורה שהרי עולתו היא וכיון דלא נפקא לחולין דתמימה היא אין קדושה חלה על מעות האבר הלכך אינה מכורה. וא"ת נמצא לוקח זה מקריב עולה חסירה אבר שאין אבר זה שלו הא פרכי' לה בפ"ק דתמורה (דף יא:) ומשנינן לה כגון דאמר הרי עלי עולה בחייה:
notes.en: Except for the payment for the limb: that he may not receive its payment. Since inherent sanctity has come upon it, he is not permitted to sell it, and if he sold it, it is not sold, since it is his burnt offering; and since it does not go out to non-sacred status, as it is unblemished, sanctity does not take effect on the money for the limb. Therefore it is not sold. And if you say: then this buyer turns out to sacrifice a burnt offering lacking a limb, since this limb is not his — this is asked in the first chapter of Temura (11b), and answered: for example, where he said, “It is incumbent upon me to bring a burnt offering in its life.”

notes.he: וא"ת וכי לוקח זה מקריב עולה חסירה אבר שאין אבר זה שלו הא פרכינן פ"ק דתמורה (דף יא:) ומשני כגון דאמר הרי עלי עולה בחייה כלומר כמו שיכול לחיות ואע"פ שנחתך רגלה מן הארכובה ולמטה והא דלא קא משני כגון דאמר רגלה של זו עולה לפטור עולתו של פלוני כמ"ד פ"ק דחולין (דף כג:) הרי עלי לחם לפטור תודתו של פלוני י"ל דלא נקט לה אלא על לשון מימרא דאמורא אבל לשון הברייתא לא מישתמע הכי:
notes.en: It is sold for the needs of a burnt offering: And if you say: does this buyer then sacrifice a burnt offering lacking a limb, since this limb is not his? This is asked in the first chapter of Temura (11b), and it answers: for example, where he said, “It is incumbent upon me to bring a burnt offering in its life,” that is, [an animal] as it can live, even though its leg was cut off from the knee joint down. And the reason it does not answer: for example, where he said, “The leg of this one is a burnt offering, to discharge the burnt offering of so-and-so,” like the one who says in the first chapter of Ḥullin (23b), “It is incumbent upon me to bring bread to discharge the thanks offering of so-and-so” — one may say that it gave that answer only to the wording of an Amora’s statement, but the wording of the baraita does not imply this.

notes.he: שהקדיש שדמיו יהא קדוש:
notes.en: Except for the payment for that limb of it: which he consecrated, that its payment shall be sacred.

messages.alt: and Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon
messages.text: From where is it derived that in the case of one who says: The leg of this animal is a burnt offering, all of the animal becomes a burnt offering? The verse states: “All that any man give of such to the Lord shall be holy.” The term “shall be” serves to include all of the animal, indicating that it all becomes sacred.

verse.he: וְאִם־בְּהֵמָה אֲשֶׁר יַקְרִיבוּ מִמֶּנָּה קׇרְבָּן לַיהֹוָה כֹּל אֲשֶׁר יִתֵּן מִמֶּנּוּ לַיהֹוָה יִהְיֶה־קֹּדֶשׁ׃
verse.en: If [the vow concerns] any animal that may be brought as an offering to GOD, any such that may be given to GOD shall be holy.

messages.text: And even according to the one, Rabbi Meir, who says that if one states: The leg of this animal is a burnt offering, not all of the animal is a burnt offering, that statement applies only if one consecrated an item that its life does not depend on, e.g., its leg. But if he consecrated an item that its life depends on, such as its head, the entire animal is consecrated.

notes.he: הכי אוקימנא בשילהי פ"ק דתמורה (דף יא:) דלא פליגי ר"מ ורבי יהודה אלא בדבר שאין הנשמה תלויה בו כגון מן הארכובה ולמטה:
notes.en: And even according to the one who says, etc.: so we established at the end of the first chapter of Temura (11b), that Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda disagree only about an item on which life does not depend, such as from the knee joint down.

messages.text: This presents a difficulty for Rava, who holds that the baraita that discusses consecration of the head is referring to items consecrated in order to purchase offerings for the altar. Why, then, isn’t the entire animal consecrated?

The Aramaic names no one in the exchange that follows. The Davidson English carries on 4b’s debate between Abaye and Rava, and Rabbeinu Gershom also names Rava; Tosafot, noting that Abaye calls him “Master,” reads Rabba, Abaye’s teacher (see the notes).

Rather, both baraitot are referring to items consecrated for the altar, and even so it is not difficult. This baraita, which indicates that if one consecrated the head the entire animal is consecrated, is referring to inherent sanctity, i.e., where he consecrated the head for the purpose of sacrificing it on the altar. That baraita, which teaches that if he consecrated the head it alone is consecrated, is referring to sanctity that inheres in its value, that is, where he consecrated the head for the sake of purchasing offerings.

notes.he: ה"ג לא קשיא ולא גרסי' אלא:
notes.en: This is our reading: “It is not difficult”; we do not read “Rather.”

notes.he: הא דקתני פשטה קדושה בכולה כגון דאקדשה קדושת הגוף דאמר ראש בהמה זו אקריב עולה וברייתא דלעיל דאין לקדשי מזבח אלא ראשה של פרה כגון דאקדשה לדמים דאמר ראש בהמה זו עלי לדמי עולה דומיא דעבד וחמור דלא שייכא בהו קדושת הגוף להקרבה:
notes.en: This one is with inherent sanctity: the baraita that teaches that the sanctity spreads through all of it is, for example, where he consecrated it with inherent sanctity, saying, “The head of this animal I will sacrifice as a burnt offering.” And the baraita above, that the consecrated property has only the head of the cow, for the altar, is where he consecrated it for its value, saying, “The head of this animal is upon me for the value of a burnt offering,” similar to a slave and a donkey, to which inherent sanctity for sacrifice does not apply.

notes.dh: הא בקדושת הגוף הא בקדושת דמים
notes.he: אי אקדשיה לראש בהמה בקדושת דמים למזבח שימכר ויקח בדמיו קרבן למזבח ודאי אין לו אלא ראשה דאפשר למכור הראש לבדו. אבל אי אקדשיה קדושת הגוף [ליקרב הוא עצמו למזבח הוא ואי אפשר לחלוק הראש מן הגוף] פשטה הקדושה בכולה דאי אפשר לשחוט הראש לשם עולה והגוף לשם חולין דהא אין שוחטין חולין בעזרה:
notes.en: This is with inherent sanctity, this with sanctity of value: if he consecrated the head of the animal with sanctity of value for the altar, that it be sold and with its money an offering be bought for the altar, certainly [the Temple] has only its head, since it is possible to sell the head alone. But if he consecrated it with inherent sanctity, [to be sacrificed itself on the altar, and it is impossible to divide the head from the body,] the sanctity spreads through all of it, since it is impossible to slaughter the head as a burnt offering and the body as non-sacred, as one does not slaughter non-sacred animals in the Temple courtyard.

messages.text: But wasn’t it you, Master, who said that if one consecrated a male animal for its value, it is sanctified with inherent sanctity and it is itself sacrificed? This undermines the distinction that Rava is attempting to draw between inherent sanctity and sanctity that inheres in value.
messages.quote: to sanctity that inheres in its value

notes.he: בפ"ק דתמורה (דף יא:) הקדיש זכר איל דחזי לעולה ואקדשיה לדמי עולה קדוש קדושת הגוף והוא עצמו יקרב עולה דמיגו דנחתא ליה קדושת דמים נחתא ליה קדושת הגוף הואיל והוא חזי לגופיה ה"נ כי אמר ראש פרה לדמי עולה תיקדש לגופה (הוא) הואיל והיא חזיא תפשוט קדושה בכולה:
notes.en: But wasn’t it the Master who said: in the first chapter of Temura (11b): if he consecrated a male, a ram, which is fit for a burnt offering, and consecrated it for the value of a burnt offering, it is sanctified with inherent sanctity, and it itself is sacrificed as a burnt offering; for since sanctity of value comes upon it, inherent sanctity comes upon it, as it is fit in itself. So too here: when he says, “The head of a cow for the value of a burnt offering,” let it be sanctified in itself, since it is fit, and let the sanctity spread through all of it.

notes.dh: והא מר הוא דאמר הקדיש זכר לדמיו
notes.he: מכאן משמע דגרסי' רבה שלא אמר אביי מר לרבא חבירו אע"ג דאשכחנא דאמר רב יוסף לאביי תלמידו מר דגברא רבה הוא ידע מאי קאמינא בזבחים פ' קדשי קדשים (זבחים דף סב.) התם שאני שהבין אביי מה שלא הבינו אחרים:
notes.en: But wasn’t it the Master who said: one who consecrates a male for its value: from here it appears that we read “Rabba” [as the one Abaye is answering], since Abaye would not call Rava, his colleague, “Master.” And although we find that Rav Yosef said to Abaye, his student, “The Master, who is a great man, knows what I am saying,” in Zevaḥim, chapter Kodshei Kodashim (62a) — there it is different, since Abaye had understood what others had not understood.

notes.he: רבא במסכת תמורה הקדיש זכר לדמיו שאמר דמי זכר זה עולה קדוש קדושת הגוף (עז) והזכר עצמו קדוש הואיל וראוי למזבח הכא נמי הואיל וראויה האי פרה לקדשי מזבח כיון דאקדשה קדושת דמים תהא קדושת מזבח ותפשוט קדושה בכולה:
notes.en: But wasn’t it the Master who said: Rava, in tractate Temura: if he consecrated a male for its value, saying, “The value of this male is a burnt offering,” it is sanctified with inherent sanctity, and the male itself is sacred, since it is fit for the altar. So too here: since this cow is fit for altar offerings, once he consecrated it with sanctity of value, let it have the sanctity of the altar, and let the sanctity spread through all of it.

messages.text: It is not difficult. This statement, that an animal that was consecrated for its value attains inherent sanctity, applies only in a case where he consecrated the entire animal. There, in the baraita discussing the consecration of the head, it is referring to a situation where he consecrated only one limb. In such a case, the animal does not attain inherent sanctity.

notes.he: לדמיו קדוש קדושת הגוף דליכא אלא חד מיגו:
notes.en: This is where he consecrated all of it: for its value, and it is sanctified with inherent sanctity, since there is only one “since” [one step of extension].

notes.he: כגון הכא דאמר ראש פרה לדמי עולה לא אמרינן מיגו דקדיש חד אבר קדשה נמי כולה ומיגו דנחתא ליה קדושת דמים נחתא ליה קדושת הגוף דתרי מיגו לא אמרינן יחד:
notes.en: This is where he consecrated one limb: as here, where he said, “The head of a cow for the value of a burnt offering.” We do not say: since one limb is sanctified, all of it is sanctified too, and since sanctity of value came upon it, inherent sanctity came upon it — for we do not say two “since”s together.

notes.he: לקדושת דמים קדשה קדושת הגוף:
notes.en: This is where he consecrated all of it: with sanctity of value, it is sanctified with inherent sanctity.

notes.he: לקדושת דמים לא קדיש קדושת הגוף:
notes.en: This is where he consecrated one limb: with sanctity of value, it is not sanctified with inherent sanctity.

messages.text: Actually, we also raised a dilemma with regard to a case where one consecrated only one limb. As Rabba raised a dilemma: If one consecrated a limb for its value in order to bring an offering with the proceeds, what is the halakha as to whether or not the entire animal is consecrated? If your interpretation of the baraita is correct, Rabba can resolve his question based on the baraita and conclude definitively that the entire animal is not sanctified for the altar.
messages.quote: where he consecrated only one limb

notes.dh: אבר נמי איבעויי איבעיא ליה למר
notes.he: בשילהי פ"ק דתמורה (דף יא:):
notes.en: [Rashi’s text reads: “About a limb, too, the Master raised a dilemma,” i.e., the one being answered raised it himself.] At the end of the first chapter of Temura (11b).

notes.he: שתקדש כל הבהמה לגופה מי אמרי' מיגו דקדיש חד אבר לדמי קדיש לגופיה ומיגו דקדיש חד אבר קדשה כולה א"ד תרי מיגו לא אמרינן ואם איתא תפשוט ליה למר מהא ברייתא דלא דהא קתני אין להקדש אלא ראשה ואוקמה לה בקדשי מזבח ודקאמר לדמי:
notes.en: If he consecrated a limb for its value, what is the halakha: is the whole animal sanctified in itself? Do we say: since one limb is sanctified for its value, it is sanctified in itself, and since one limb is sanctified, all of it is sanctified? Or perhaps we do not say two “since”s? And if [your distinction] is right, let the Master resolve it from this baraita, that it is not, since it teaches, “The consecrated property has only its head,” and we established it as dealing with items consecrated for the altar, where he said “for its value.”

notes.he: מי קדש קדושת דמים או קדושת הגוף דומיא דחמור דלא קרב למזבח:
notes.en: What is the halakha: is it sanctified with sanctity of value or with inherent sanctity? Similar to a donkey, which is not sacrificed on the altar.

messages.text: We raised this dilemma and entertained the possibility that the entire animal might be sanctified to the altar only in a case where the animal is unblemished, and is therefore fit to be used as an offering. But here, the baraita is referring to a blemished animal, similar to the parallel case of the donkey, which is unfit to be sacrificed. Since the animal in question is unfit for the altar, it is clear that the entire animal is not sanctified.

notes.he: דאיכא למימר דתיחות ליה קדושת הגוף דהא חזי להקרבה וברייתא דפשיטא ליה דלא קדשה כולה בבעל מום קא מיירי דומיא דעבד וחמור דלא חזו לגופייהו:
notes.en: With an unblemished one: where one could say that inherent sanctity comes upon it, since it is fit for sacrifice. And the baraita, for which it is obvious that not all of it is sanctified, speaks of a blemished animal, similar to a slave and a donkey, which are not fit in themselves.

messages.text: In fact, we also raised a dilemma with regard to a case where the animal is blemished and unfit to be sacrificed. As Rabba raised a dilemma: If one said: It is incumbent upon me to donate the value of my head to purchase offerings to be sacrificed on the altar, what is the halakha? Is he obligated in his entire value or not? A person is certainly not fit to be an offering, and yet Rabba does not resolve his question based on the baraita.
messages.quote: here, the baraita is referring to a blemished animal

notes.he: אין לך בעל מום לגבי מזבח יותר מאדם]:
notes.en: The value of my head for the altar: you have nothing more blemished, as far as the altar is concerned, than a person.

messages.text: We only raised this dilemma before hearing this baraita. Now that we have heard this baraita, we no longer raise this dilemma, as we concluded from the baraita that the entirety of the animal is not consecrated.

notes.dh: דבעי רבה דמי ראשי לגבי מזבח כו' תיקו
notes.he: היינו מקמי דלשמעינן מתני' דלעיל כדמסקינן:
notes.en: As Rabba raised a dilemma: “The value of my head for the altar,” etc., and it remained “let it stand”: that was before we heard the baraita above, as we conclude.

notes.he: ראש חמור:
notes.en: Before we heard this baraita: about the head of a donkey.

messages.text: If one said: It is incumbent upon me to donate the value of my head to purchase offerings to be sacrificed on the altar, what is the halakha? Is it assessed by the significance of the body part in question, and since he consecrated a vital organ he is obligated in his entire value? Or perhaps it is not assessed by the significance of the body part in question, and only the head is consecrated.
messages.lead: § The Gemara returns to the aforementioned matter itself. Rabba raised a dilemma:

notes.dh: דמי ראשי למזבח מי נידון בכבודו או אין נידון בכבודו
notes.he: ויהיב פלגא דמים והרי אין לך בעל מום למזבח גדול מזה שהוא אדם וקא מיבעיא ליה ואמאי תיפשוט ליה מההיא דאין נידון:
notes.en: “The value of my head for the altar”: is he assessed by its significance, or is he not assessed by its significance and gives half the value? And you have nothing more blemished, as far as the altar is concerned, than this, since he is a person; and yet he raises a dilemma about it. Why? Let him resolve it from that [baraita], that he is not assessed [by its significance].

notes.he: (בעי רבה דמי ראשי למזבח -) צריך עיון אמאי לא נקט ערך ראשי לגבי מזבח כמו בבעיא דבסמוך:
notes.en: (Rabba raised a dilemma: the value of my head for the altar.) This requires study: why did he not put it as “the valuation of my head for the altar,” as in the dilemma that follows?

notes.he: דאבר ויהיב דמי כוליה גופיה למזבח:
notes.en: Assessed by its significance: that of the limb, and he gives the value of his whole body to the altar.

messages.text: It can be argued that we have not found a case of assessments that is not assessed by the significance of the body part that was specified. Therefore, if one obligated himself in the value of a vital organ he should have to pay the entity’s entire value.

notes.he: נדר בשום דוכתא דאין נידון בכבודו א"ד לא אשכחן לגבי מזבח כו':
notes.en: Do we say we have not found: a vow anywhere that is not assessed by its significance; or perhaps we have not found for the altar, etc.

messages.text:
Or perhaps he should be obligated only in the value of the head, as we have not found a case of an animal that is sacrificed on the altar that is assessed by the significance of the body part in question, i.e., that if one consecrates the value of one vital organ the entire animal is consecrated.
The dilemma shall stand [teiku] unresolved.

notes.he: דקדוש בערכין דאין נידון בכבודו או דלמא לא אשכחן בעל מום לגבי מזבח דנידון בכבודו וכדתרצינן (התם) [הכא] בבעל מום דומיא דחמור:
notes.en: We have not found: [anything] sanctified in valuations that is not assessed by its significance; or perhaps we have not found a blemished thing, for the altar, that is assessed by its significance, as we answered here: with a blemished animal, similar to a donkey.

messages.text: If one said: It is incumbent upon me to donate my valuation for the altar, rather than for Temple maintenance, as is usually the case, what is the halakha? Is this case determined based on affordability if he is poor, like regular valuations? Or perhaps it is not determined based on affordability, and he is obligated in the full valuation even if he is poor.

notes.he: גבי נדר ונדבה כי האי:
notes.en: Assessed by affordability: with regard to a vow or a gift such as this.

notes.dh: בעי רבא ערכי עלי לגבי מזבח
notes.he: אי רבה גרסי' בכולן יש לפרש באם תמצא לומר כדלעיל:
notes.en: Rava raised a dilemma: “My valuation is upon me for the altar”: if we read “Rabba” in all of them, one can explain it as an “if you say” [that builds on the dilemma] above.

notes.he: כדאמרן לעיל]:
notes.en: Assessed by affordability: as we said above.

messages.text:
One can argue that we have not found a case of valuations that is not determined based on affordability. Therefore, the principle of affordability should apply even when one vows for the purpose of sacrificing offerings on the altar. Or perhaps this case should not be determined based on affordability, as we have not found an item that is consecrated for the purpose of sacrificing offerings on the altar that is redeemed in a manner other than according to its value.
The dilemma shall stand unresolved.

If a person consecrated an ancestral field for the purpose of sacrificing offerings on the altar, rather than for Temple maintenance, as is usually the case, what is the halakha? Do we say that we have not found a case of an ancestral field that is redeemed other than by the standard rate established by the Torah, which is that an area fit for the sowing of a ḥomer, a kor, of barley seed is redeemed for fifty silver shekels?

notes.he: לדמי עולה:
notes.en: If he consecrated an ancestral field: for the value of a burnt offering.

notes.he: היכי פריק ליה אי בעי למיפרקיה דהא פשיטא לן אי אקדשיה לבדק הבית הוה פריק בית זרע חומר שעורים בחמשים שקל כסף דגזירת הכתוב הוא ואפילו היא שוה אלף זוז:
notes.en: What is the halakha: how does he redeem it, if he wants to redeem it? For it is obvious to us that had he consecrated it for Temple maintenance, he would redeem it at an area for sowing a ḥomer of barley for fifty silver shekels, as it is a decree of the verse, even if it is worth a thousand zuz.

messages.text: Or perhaps it should be redeemed according to its market value, as we have not found a case of an item that is consecrated for the purpose of sacrificing offerings on the altar that is redeemed in a manner other than according to its value.

notes.he: דהא לא אשכחן שדה אחוזה אלא לבדק הבית דסתם הקדישות לבדק הבית הלכך כי פריש לה למזבח לא פריק לה נמי אלא בהכי או דלמא לא אשכחן למזבח אלא בשויו דהא לא אשכחן קראי למזבח אלא בבהמות והנהו ודאי לא נתנה תורה קצבה לפדיונן אם הוממו והכא נמי אמרינן בשויו. תיקו:
notes.en: An ancestral field that is redeemed: for we have found an ancestral field only for Temple maintenance, since unspecified consecrations are for Temple maintenance. Therefore, when he designates it for the altar, he also redeems it only in this way. Or perhaps we have found the altar only at its value, since we have found verses about the altar only concerning animals, and for those the Torah certainly did not set a fixed sum for their redemption if they became blemished; so here too we say: at its value. Let it stand.

messages.text: Once again: The dilemma shall stand unresolved.

messages.caption: Three pledges for the altar, each caught between two rules “we have not found” an exception to. All three are left standing (teiku).

messages.text: Mishna

A child less than one month old is the object of a vow if others vowed to donate his assessment, but is not valuated if one vowed to donate his fixed value, as the Torah did not establish a value for anyone less than a month old.

notes.he: אם אמר אחר דמיו עלי שהרי דמים כל דהו יש לו:
notes.en: Mishna: Less than one month old is the object of a vow: if another said, “His value is upon me,” since he has some value, however small.

notes.he: שלא נאמר בפרשה אלא מבן חודש ומעלה:
notes.en: But is not valuated: since the passage speaks only of “from a month old and upward.”

messages.text: Gemara
The person who valuated is obligated to give the child’s assessment.
messages.lead: The Sages taught in a baraita: With regard to a case of one who takes a vow of valuation concerning a child less than one month old,

notes.he: כמה שהוא נמכר בשוק:
notes.en: Gemara: He gives his assessment: what he would sell for in the market.

notes.he: שוויו:
notes.en: He gives his assessment: his worth.

messages.text: He has said nothing, i.e., he is not obligated to give anything.

With regard to what principle do they disagree? Rabbi Meir holds: A person does not issue his statement of consecration for naught. The assumption is that a person knows that there are no valuations for a child less than one month old, and therefore he intended and said his statement for the sake of assessments, i.e., he meant to vow to give the child’s market value.
And the Rabbis hold that a person does make his statement of consecration for naught. Therefore, his statement is taken at face value, and he is not obligated to give anything.
In accordance with whose opinion is that which Rav Giddel says that Rav says?
One who says: It is incumbent upon me to donate the valuation of this utensil, is obligated to give its assessment.

It is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Meir, who holds that a person does not issue a statement of consecration for naught. Since utensils are not subject to valuation, he presumably intended to obligate himself in its assessment.
messages.quote: valuation of this utensil, is obligated to give its assessment

notes.he: דאמר אין אדם מוציא דבריו לבטלה ואדם יודע דאין ערך לכלי דנפשות כתיב וגמר ואמר לשם דמים:
notes.en: In accordance with Rabbi Meir: who says a person does not utter his words for naught; and a person knows there is no valuation for a utensil, since “persons” is written [in the passage], so he decided and spoke for the sake of assessment.

notes.he: דאין ערך לכלי מן התורה. נותן דמיו. כר' מאיר דאמר אין אדם מוציא דבריו לבטלה:
notes.en: One who says, “The valuation of a utensil is upon me”: since there is no valuation for a utensil by Torah law. He gives its assessment: in accordance with Rabbi Meir, who says a person does not utter his words for naught.

messages.text: Isn’t it obvious that Rav’s statement is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Meir? Why was it necessary for the Gemara to state this?

notes.he: ל"ל למימר כמאן אזלא הא:
notes.en: It is obvious that it is in accordance with Rabbi Meir: why do I need to say, “In accordance with whom is this?”

messages.text: It was necessary to state that Rav’s statement is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Meir, lest you say that it is even in accordance with the opinion of the Rabbis, who exempt one who valuates a child under a month old. One could say that it is only there, in the case of the child, that one errs and thinks that just as there are valuations for a child who is one month old, there are also valuations for a child less than one month old. Since his vow was based on an error, he is not obligated to pay anything.

notes.he: גבי פחות מבן חדש פטרי רבנן משום דאיכא למימר אפילו אין אדם מוציא דבריו לבטלה הני מילי היכא דהוא יודע שדבריו בטילין אבל זה סבור היה שיש ערך לפחות מבן חדש כבן חדש והרי אין לו ונמצא הקדש טעות ודמים לא קאמר דליתיב דמי אבל גבי כלי ליחייב קמ"ל דר"מ היא ולא רבנן דטעמייהו דרבנן משום דאדם מוציא דבריו לבטלה ואפילו הוא יודע שדבריו זה בטילין:
notes.en: There: with one less than a month old, the Rabbis exempt him, because one could say: even if a person does not utter his words for naught, that applies only where he knows his words are void. But this one thought there was a valuation for one less than a month old, as for one a month old, and there is none; so it turns out to be a consecration made in error, and he did not speak of value, that he should give the value. But with a utensil, let him be liable. It teaches us that it is Rabbi Meir’s view and not the Rabbis’, since the Rabbis’ reason is that a person does utter his words for naught, even when he knows that these words of his are void.

messages.text: But here, in the case of one who valuates a utensil, where there is no possibility of erring, it can be argued that a person certainly knows that there is no valuation for a utensil, and he therefore intended and said his statement for the sake of assessments, i.e., he meant to vow to donate the utensil’s value.

notes.dh: אדם יודע שאין ערך לפחות מבן חדש
notes.he: ואפילו אינו יודע מ"מ דעתו ע"פ שתקנו חכמים הלשון וא"ת מאי שנא מדאמר פרק תמיד נשחט (פסחים דף סג.) המתכוין לומר תרומה ואמר מעשר מעשר ואמר תרומה לא אמר כלום ויש לומר דלא אמר כלום ממה שמוציא בפיו אבל מה שבלבו הוי קיים ועוד יש לומר דהתם שאני שמה שאמר בפיו אינו רוצה ובמה שאמר בלבו טעה:
notes.en: A person knows there is no valuation for one less than a month old: and even if he does not know, in any case his intention follows the language the Sages established. And if you say: how is this different from what is said in the chapter Tamid Nishḥat (Pesaḥim 63a): one who intends to say “teruma” and said “tithe,” or “tithe” and said “teruma,” has said nothing? One may say: he has said nothing by what he utters with his mouth, but what is in his heart stands. Alternatively, one may say: there it is different, since what he said with his mouth he does not want, and in what he said in his heart he erred.

messages.text: Therefore, the Gemara teaches us that Rav’s statement is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Meir only, and not with that of the Rabbis. The Rabbis hold that a person does issue a statement of consecration for naught even in such a case, and therefore his declaration is taken at face value.
5b

And as Rav stated his halakha in accordance with Rabbi Meir, who says that one who valuates a child less than a month old must pay his assessment, for what reason was it necessary for Rav to state his ruling? Isn’t this obvious?

notes.he: הואיל ורב אליבא דר"מ אמר ולא לרבנן למאי איצטריך למימר דנותן דמיו פשיטא התם דאיכא למימר דטעה ולא אמר לשם דמים אלא סבור שיש לו ערך מחייב רבי מאיר הכא דודאי יודע שאין ערך לכלי לא כ"ש:
notes.en: And according to Rabbi Meir, why is it necessary: since Rav spoke according to Rabbi Meir and not according to the Rabbis, why was it necessary to say that he gives its value? It is obvious: there, where one could say he erred and did not speak for the sake of value but thought there was a valuation, Rabbi Meir holds him liable; here, where he certainly knows there is no valuation for a utensil, all the more so.

notes.he: מאי דסבירא ליה בערך פחות מבן חדש סבירא ליה בערך כלי ולר' מאיר אמאי איצטריך. הא דרב גידל הא אשמעינן חדא זימנא דאין אדם מוציא דבריו לבטלה:
notes.en: It is obvious: what he holds about the valuation of one less than a month old, he holds about the valuation of a utensil. And according to Rabbi Meir, why was it needed? This ruling of Rav Giddel: he already taught us once that a person does not utter his words for naught.

messages.text: It was necessary for him to state this halakha, lest you say that the reason that Rabbi Meir obligates him to pay the assessment there, in the case of the child, is that he decrees one must pay if the child is less than a month old, due to concern that otherwise people might mistakenly refrain from paying the valuation of a child who is a month old. But here, in the case of one who valuates a utensil, where there is no cause for such an error and therefore no need to decree, one might say that Rabbi Meir would not obligate him to pay.

notes.he: ס"ד טעמא דר' מאיר דגזר ערך פחות מבן חדש אטו בן חדש דאי פטרת ליה מערכין פחות מבן חדש זימנין דמעריך בן חדש וסבר הכי נמי פטרנא. אבל בערך כלי דליכא למיטעא אימא לא ליתן דמיו קמ"ל:
notes.en: One might have thought Rabbi Meir’s reason is that he decreed about the valuation of one less than a month old because of one a month old: for if you exempt him from the valuation of one less than a month old, sometimes he will valuate one a month old and think, “I am exempt here too.” But with the valuation of a utensil, where there is no room for error, say he does not give its value. It teaches us [otherwise].

messages.text: Therefore, Rav teaches us that since the reason of Rabbi Meir is that a person does not make his statement of consecration for naught, there is no difference between here, the case of a child, and there, with regard to a utensil. Rather, the halakha is the same in both cases.
In accordance with whose opinion is that which Rabba bar Yosef says that Rav says, and some say that Rav Yeiva bar Yosei says that Rav says?

messages.alt: and some say Rav Yeiva bar Yosei says that Rav says
messages.text: One who consecrates the animal of another must give its assessment.

notes.he: דאדם יודע שאין הקדש חל על דבר שאינו שלו וגמר ואמר לשם דמים:
notes.en: He gives its assessment: for a person knows that consecration does not take effect on something that is not his, so he decided and spoke for the sake of value.

messages.text: In accordance with whom? It is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Meir, that one does not issue a statement of consecration for naught. Since he knows that he cannot consecrate that which is not his, he meant to obligate himself in the animal’s assessment.
messages.quote: One who consecrates the animal of another

notes.he: דהכא נמי נימא אדם יודע שאין אדם מקדיש בהמה שאינה שלו וגמר ואמר לשום דמים:
notes.en: In accordance with whom? Rabbi Meir: here too we say a person knows that one cannot consecrate an animal that is not his, so he decided and spoke for the sake of value.

messages.text: But didn’t Rav already say it once? As Rav Giddel says that Rav says: One who says: It is incumbent upon me to donate the valuation of a utensil, must give its assessment.
messages.quote: valuation of this utensil, is obligated to give its assessment

messages.text: Rav found it necessary to issue both statements, lest you say that this halakha applies only there, with regard to a utensil, as a person knows that a utensil has no valuation, i.e., that the term: Valuation, is not relevant to a utensil, and therefore it must be that he decided to donate money and says this expression as a reference to its monetary value, using the term: Valuation, imprecisely.

But in the case where one obligated himself in the valuation of another’s animal, which is subject to consecration, albeit not by him, there is room to say that this is what he is saying to himself: Were I to say to the owner that I want to buy it, he would sell it to me. Therefore, let it be consecrated from now, and I will sacrifice it once I purchase it from him. His intent is to consecrate the animal itself in order to sacrifice it. But since he did not say to himself that he would give its assessment, his statement is meaningless, as one cannot consecrate property that does not belong to him.

notes.he: כשאקננה ולהקדיש גופה נתכוין דטעה בהכי אבל דמי לא קאמר הלכך לא ליתיב מידי דהא אין הקדישו חל על גופה ולדמים לא נתכוין:
notes.en: Let it be consecrated from now, and I will sacrifice it: when I buy it. He intended to consecrate the animal itself, erring in this, but he did not speak of value. Therefore let him give nothing, since his consecration does not take effect on the animal itself, and he did not intend its value.

notes.he: אע"ג שאינה שלי לכשאקחנה אקרבה ולא מקדשה לדמיה אלא אדעתה למיקרבה ולא קדשה לא להקרבה ולא לדמים קמ"ל דקדשה לדמים]:
notes.en: Let it be consecrated from now: even though it is not mine, when I buy it I will sacrifice it. He does not consecrate it for its value but has in mind to sacrifice it, and it is sanctified neither for sacrifice nor for value. It teaches us that it is sanctified for value.

messages.text: Therefore, Rav teaches us that this is not the case. Rather, his statement should be interpreted in such a manner that he is obligated to give the assessment of the animal to the Temple treasury.

notes.he: דלא אמרי' דטעה אלא ודאי יודע שאין הקדישו חל על גופה ולדמים נתכוין:
notes.en: It teaches us: that we do not say he erred; rather, he certainly knows that his consecration does not take effect on the animal itself, and he intended its value.

messages.text: And Rav’s ruling applies only in a case where one says: It is incumbent upon me to donate to the Temple treasury. But if he says: This animal is consecrated, he is not obligated to pay its assessment. This formulation clearly indicates that he intended to consecrate this animal, which he cannot do, as it does not yet belong to him.
messages.quote: One who consecrates the animal of another must give its assessment

notes.he: דמי בהמת חבירו זו עלי להקריב נותן דמים דבהמה גופה לא קאמר אבל דמים קיבל עליו:
notes.en: And that is where he said “upon me”: [he said,] “The value of this animal of my fellow is upon me, to sacrifice”; he gives its value, since he did not speak of the animal itself but took its value upon himself.

notes.he: ולא אמר עלי אלא אמר הרי בהמה זו עולה לא אמר כלום:
notes.en: But if he said “this”: and did not say “upon me,” but said, “This animal is a burnt offering,” he has said nothing.

notes.he: כשאמר על בהמת חברו בהמה זו עלי הקדש נותן דמיה אבל אמר בהמה זו הקדש פטור מכלום דאין אדם מקדיש דבר שאינו שלו:
notes.en: And that is where he said “upon me”: when he said of his fellow’s animal, “This animal is upon me as consecrated property,” he gives its value. But if he said, “This animal is consecrated property,” he is exempt from everything, since a person cannot consecrate what is not his.

messages.text: Mishna

He is valuated in a case where a Jew says: It is incumbent upon me to donate the fixed value of this gentile. But a gentile does not take a vow of valuation to donate his fixed value or the value of others.

notes.he: אם אמר ישראל ערכו עלי נותן ערכו כפי שנים של עובד כוכבים:
notes.en: Mishna: A gentile is valuated: if a Jew said, “His valuation is upon me,” he gives the valuation according to the gentile’s years.

notes.he: אבל אם אמר העובד כוכבים ערכי עלי או ערך אחרים עלי לא אמר כלום:
notes.en: But does not valuate: but if the gentile said, “My valuation is upon me” or “The valuation of others is upon me,” he has said nothing.

messages.text: He takes a vow of valuation, but is not valuated.

notes.he: אם אמר על ישראל ערכו עלי:
notes.en: Rabbi Yehuda says: He valuates: if he said of a Jew, “His valuation is upon me.”

notes.he: שאם אמר ערכי עלי אין לו ערך או אם אמר ישראל ערך עובד כוכבים זה עלי לא אמר כלום:
notes.en: But is not valuated: for if he said, “My valuation is upon me,” he has no valuation; or if a Jew said, “The valuation of this gentile is upon me,” he has said nothing.

messages.text: And both this tanna, Rabbi Meir, and that tanna, Rabbi Yehuda, agree that gentiles vow to donate the assessment of another and are the object of vows, whereby one donates the assessment of a gentile.
Gemara

It is written in the beginning of the passage in the Torah delineating valuations: “Speak to the children of Israel.” This teaches that “the children of Israel” can take a vow of valuation, but gentiles cannot take a vow of valuation.
messages.lead: The Sages taught the following in a baraita that deals with the reasoning for the rulings of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda:

verse.he: דַּבֵּר אֶל־בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאָמַרְתָּ אֲלֵהֶם אִישׁ כִּי יַפְלִא נֶדֶר בְּעֶרְכְּךָ נְפָשֹׁת לַיהֹוָה׃
verse.en: Speak to the Israelite people and say to them: When anyone explicitly vows to GOD the equivalent for a human being,

messages.text: One might have thought that this means that gentiles cannot be the object of a valuation either. Therefore, the verse states the inclusive expression: “When a man shall clearly utter a vow of persons to the Lord, according to your valuation,” to teach that in this regard, every “man,” even a gentile, is included in halakhot of valuations. This is the statement of Rabbi Meir.

notes.dh: יכול לא יהו נערכין ת"ל איש
notes.he: ואע"ג דאיש במעריך כתיב תרתי איש כתיבי ואם אינו ענין למעריך תנהו לענין נערך וא"ת הא ממעטינן מאיש דהכא עובדי כוכבים גבי תמורה בפ"ק דתמורה (דף ג.) וי"ל דבפרק ב"ש במסכת זבחים (דף מה.) איכא דרשא אחריתי למעוטי עובדי כוכבים דתמורה ועלה סמיך וילפינן ממעשר בהמה חובה שאין קבועה לה זמן וישראל מייתו ועובדי כוכבים לא מייתו:
notes.en: One might have thought they are not valuated; the verse states “a man”: And although “a man” is written of the one who valuates, “a man” is written twice; if it is not needed for the one who valuates, apply it to the one who is valuated. And if you say: but in the first chapter of Temura (3a) we exclude gentiles from substitution by this very “a man”? One may say that in the chapter Beit Shammai in tractate Zevaḥim (45a) there is another exposition excluding gentiles from substitution, and it relies on that one: we derive it from the animal tithe, an obligatory offering with no fixed time, which Jews bring and gentiles do not.

messages.text: Since one verse, “a man,” includes gentiles, and another verse, “the children of Israel,” excludes gentiles, for what reason do I say that a gentile can be the object of a valuation but cannot take a vow of valuation, rather than the reverse?

notes.he: כלומר איש מרבה עובדי כוכבים ובני ישראל ממעיט מפני מה כו':
notes.en: Since one verse, etc.: that is, “a man” includes gentiles and “the children of Israel” excludes them; for what reason, etc.

messages.text: It is due to the fact that the verse included more people in the category of those who are the object of a valuation than in the category of those who take a vow of valuation. As the mishna teaches (2a): A deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor are the object of a vow and are valuated, but they can neither vow to donate the assessment of a person nor take a vow of valuation.

“The children of Israel,” can be the object of a valuation but gentiles cannot be the object of a valuation. One might have thought that gentiles cannot take a vow of valuation either. Therefore, the verse states the inclusive expression: “A man,” to teach that in this regard, every “man,” even a gentile, is included in the halakha of valuations.
messages.lead: Interpreting the verses in the reverse manner:

verse.he: דַּבֵּר אֶל־בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאָמַרְתָּ אֲלֵהֶם אִישׁ כִּי יַפְלִא נֶדֶר בְּעֶרְכְּךָ נְפָשֹׁת לַיהֹוָה׃
verse.en: Speak to the Israelite people and say to them: When anyone explicitly vows to GOD the equivalent for a human being,

notes.he: משמע כל דהו:
notes.en: Gemara: “A man”: implies anyone at all.

messages.text: Since one verse, “a man,” includes gentiles, and another verse, “the children of Israel,” excludes gentiles, for what reason do I say that a gentile can take a vow of a valuation but cannot be the object of a valuation? It is due to the fact that the verse included more people in the category of those who take a vow of valuation than in the category of those who are the object of a valuation. As the mishna teaches (2a): A tumtum and a hermaphrodite vow, are the object of a vow, and take vows of valuation, but they are not valuated.

notes.he: במעריכין יותר מן הנערכין שהרי טומטום ואנדרוגינוס מעריכין אבל לא נערכין:
notes.en: Because the verse included: more among those who valuate than among those who are valuated, since a tumtum and a hermaphrodite valuate but are not valuated.

notes.he: ואי אמרת אוקי חרש שוטה וקטן כנגד טומטום ואנדרוגינוס והוו להו נערכין טפי ממעריכין הא לא קשיא [כולהי תלת] חרש שוטה וקטן חשיבי להו כחד דלית בהו דעה ועוד ריבה [במעריכין] עובדי כוכבים יותר מבנערכין שהרי טומטום ואנדרוגינוס נודרין ונידרין ומעריכין ועובד כוכבים [נמי] נודר ונידר [הלכך עדיף] לאפוקי חרש שוטה וקטן דאינן נידרין:
notes.en: And if you say: set the deaf-mute, the imbecile and the minor against the tumtum and the hermaphrodite, and those who are valuated come out more than those who valuate — this is not difficult: [all three,] the deaf-mute, the imbecile and the minor, count as one, since they lack understanding. Moreover, [the verse] included gentiles more [among those who valuate] than among those who are valuated, since the tumtum and the hermaphrodite vow, are the object of vows, and valuate, and a gentile [too] vows and is the object of vows; [therefore it is preferable,] to the exclusion of the deaf-mute, the imbecile and the minor, who are not the object of vows. [So the text reads; the mishna on 2a says they are the object of vows but do not vow.]

messages.caption: A gentile and valuations: what Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda rule, the precedent each brings, and Rava’s verdict on each.

messages.text: Rabbi Meir’s halakha is reasonable, but his explanation is not reasonable. Conversely, Rabbi Yehuda’s explanation is reasonable, but his halakha is not reasonable.

notes.he: [מימרא דר' מאיר] נראה עיקר [טעמו אין נראה עיקר:
notes.en: Rabbi Meir’s halakha is reasonable: [Rabbi Meir’s ruling] appears correct; [his reason does not appear correct.]

messages.text: Rabbi Meir’s halakha that gentiles cannot take a valuation vow is reasonable, as it is written that the Jews who returned to Eretz Yisrael from Babylonia rejected the Samaritans’ request to assist them in the construction of the Second Temple, saying: “You have nothing to do with us to build a house to our God.” This supports Rabbi Meir’s contention that gentiles may not take vows of valuation, which are used for Temple maintenance.
messages.quote: A deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor

verse.he: וַיֹּאמֶר לָהֶם זְרֻבָּבֶל וְיֵשׁוּעַ וּשְׁאָר רָאשֵׁי הָאָבוֹת לְיִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא־לָכֶם וָלָנוּ לִבְנוֹת בַּיִת לֵאלֹהֵינוּ כִּי אֲנַחְנוּ יַחַד נִבְנֶה לַיהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּנוּ הַמֶּלֶךְ כּוֹרֶשׁ מֶלֶךְ־פָּרָס׃
verse.en: Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the rest of the heads of the clans of Israel answered them, “It is not for you and us to build a House to our God, but we alone will build it to the ETERNAL God of Israel, in accord with the charge that the king, King Cyrus of Persia, laid upon us.”

notes.he: דאין העובדי כוכבים מעריכין:
notes.en: Rabbi Meir’s halakha is reasonable: that gentiles do not valuate.

notes.he: דאינו מעריך דכתיב] לא לכם ולנו לבנות בית כלומר הנהו סנבלט וטוביה דהוו עובדי כוכבים לא הניחום לבנות ולהקדיש לצורך בדק הבית:
notes.en: [Rabbi Meir’s halakha is reasonable: that he does not valuate, since] it is written, “You have nothing to do with us to build a house”: that is, those men, Sanballat and Toviya, who were gentiles — they did not let them build and consecrate for the needs of Temple maintenance.

notes.he: אלמא דעובדי כוכבים אין מעריכין דערכין נמי לבדק הבית הן אבל נערכין שישראל יכול להעריכן דהוי ממון ישראל:
notes.en: Evidently gentiles do not valuate, since valuations too are for Temple maintenance. But they are valuated, since a Jew can valuate them, as it is a Jew’s money.

messages.text: But his explanation is not reasonable, as he adduces proof for his halakha from the fact that a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor cannot take a vow of valuation. This proof is unconvincing, since a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor are different, as unlike gentiles, they lack the presumed mental competence to make a commitment.

notes.he: דיליף טעמא מחרש שוטה וקטן ואיכא למיפרך התם משום דלאו בני דעה נינהו דהא אין נודרין נמי ואין מקדישין אבל עובד כוכבים דנודר ומקדיש דהא ר"מ מודה דנודר ונידר אימא נמי דמעריך אי לאו דהאי קרא דלא לכם ולנו דכתיב בספר עזרא שהיו עובדי כוכבים מתנדבין ורוצין לסייען בבנין בית שני ואמר להם נחמיה בן חכליה לא לכם ולנו לבנות כי אם לנו לבדנו:
notes.en: And his reason is not reasonable: since he derives his reason from a deaf-mute, an imbecile and a minor, and one can refute this: there, it is because they are not competent, since they also do not vow and do not consecrate. But a gentile, who does vow and consecrate — for Rabbi Meir concedes that he vows and is the object of vows — say that he also valuates, were it not for this verse, “You have nothing to do with us,” written in the book of Ezra, where the gentiles were volunteering and wanted to help them build the Second Temple, and Neḥemya son of Ḥakhalya said to them: “You have nothing to do with us to build; rather, we alone.” [In Ezra 4:3 the reply is given by Zerubbabel, Jeshua and the heads of the fathers’ houses.]

notes.dh: שאני חרש שוטה וקטן דלאו בני דעה נינהו
notes.he: ור"מ דיליף מינייהו סבירא ליה קצת הן שוין הואיל ונערכין ואע"פ שלא מעריכין הכי נמי אית ליה למימר בעובדי כוכבים:
notes.en: A deaf-mute, an imbecile and a minor are different, since they are not competent: and Rabbi Meir, who derives from them, holds that they are somewhat alike, since they are valuated even though they do not valuate; so too he can say of gentiles.

notes.dh: [טעמיה לא מסתברא דקא מייתי לה מחרש שוטה וקטן
notes.he: דקאמר שהרי חרש שוטה וקטן נערכין ולא מעריכין דלמא משום הכי לא מעריכין דלאו בני דעה נינהו אבל עובד כוכבים דבן דעת הוא איכא למימר דמעריך:
notes.en: [His reason is not reasonable, since he brings it from a deaf-mute, an imbecile and a minor:] for he says that a deaf-mute, an imbecile and a minor are valuated but do not valuate. Perhaps they do not valuate because they are not competent; but a gentile, who is competent, one could say does valuate.

messages.text: By contrast, Rabbi Yehuda’s explanation is reasonable, in that he adduces proof for his halakha from the case of a tumtum and a hermaphrodite, as even though they possess the presumed mental competence to make a commitment, nevertheless the Merciful One excludes them from being valuated. Since they are comparable to gentiles, they can serve as a precedent.

notes.he: דודאי מסתבר טפי לאוקמא מיעוטא דממעיט קרא בנערכין וריבויא במעריכין דהא טומטום ואנדרוגינוס דבני דעה נינהו כעובדי כוכבים ומעריכין ולא נערכין דמעטינהו קרא דכתיב הזכר מריבויא דה"י דרשינן זכר ודאי ולא טומטום ואנדרוגינוס:
notes.en: Rabbi Yehuda’s reason is reasonable: for it is certainly more reasonable to apply the exclusion the verse makes to those who are valuated, and the inclusion to those who valuate, since the tumtum and the hermaphrodite, who are competent like gentiles, valuate but are not valuated, for the verse excluded them, as it is written, “the male” (Leviticus 27:3): from the extra letter heh we expound, a definite male, and not a tumtum or a hermaphrodite.

notes.he: דאע"ג דבני דעה נינהו מעטינהו רחמנא מנערכין משום זכר ודאי ונקבה ודאית אבל מעריכין דבני דעה נינהו אף עובדי כוכבים נמי כיון דבני דיעה נינהו מעריכין אבל לא נערכין דהא מעטינהו רחמנא נמי מבני ישראל:
notes.en: Since he brings it from a tumtum and a hermaphrodite: although they are competent, the Merciful One excluded them from being valuated, because [the verse requires] a definite male and a definite female. But as for valuating, since they are competent, [they valuate]; gentiles too, since they are competent, valuate, but are not valuated, since the Merciful One excluded them too, by “the children of Israel.”

messages.text: But his halakha that gentiles can take a valuation vow is not reasonable, as it is written: “You have nothing to do with us to build a house to our God,” which indicates that they may not contribute anything to Temple maintenance.

notes.he: דודאי אין מעריך משום דערכין לבדק הבית וקרא כתיב לא לכם ולנו לבנות:
notes.en: And his halakha is not reasonable: for he certainly does not valuate, since valuations are for Temple maintenance, and the verse writes, “You have nothing to do with us to build.”

notes.he: דהא כתיב לא לכם ולנו:
notes.en: His halakha is not reasonable: since it is written, “You have nothing to do with us.”

messages.text: And Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that gentiles can take valuation vows and that the funds go to Temple maintenance, what does he do with this verse: “You have nothing to do with us”?
He derives from it that if a gentile takes a vow of valuation and he brings the money to the Temple, his valuation money is not utilized but rather is interred.
messages.quote: what does he do with this verse

notes.he: הא דאמר רבי יהודה מעריכין לאו משום דליתיה לבדק הבית דהא כתיב לא לכם ולנו אלא קדוש ונגנז דאסור בהנאה:
notes.en: Avimi said: that Rabbi Yehuda said they valuate is not because it goes to Temple maintenance, since it is written, “You have nothing to do with us”; rather, it is sacred and interred, as it is forbidden for benefit.

notes.he: משמע דאין ערכן נכנס לבדק הבית. קסבר ר' יהודה אין ודאי מעריכין אמר רב חסדא וערכן נגנז שלא יפול לבדק הבית משום דכתיב לא לכם ולנו:
notes.en: What does he do with it: implying that their valuation does not enter Temple maintenance. Rabbi Yehuda holds that they certainly valuate; Rav Ḥisda said: and their valuation is interred, so that it does not fall to Temple maintenance, since it is written, “You have nothing to do with us.”

messages.text: If that is so, that the valuation is not utilized for the Temple, one who uses it should not be considered to have violated the prohibition of misuse. One who unwittingly derived benefit from the valuation should not be obligated to bring a guilt offering for misuse of consecrated property, as the Temple treasury does not derive benefit from it.
messages.quote: his valuation money is not utilized but rather is interred

notes.he: הואיל ולאיבוד אזיל לא ימעלו בו דמיתהני מיניה לא ניחייב קרבן מעילה דהא תנן חטאות המתות הני חטאות דאמרי' בתמורה ולד חטאת ותמורת חטאת כו':
notes.en: If that is so: since it goes to destruction, let one not be liable for misuse of it: one who benefits from it should not be liable to bring a misuse offering, for we learned: sin offerings left to die — the sin offerings listed in Temura: the offspring of a sin offering, the substitute of a sin offering, etc.

notes.he: לרבי יהודה אלמה תניא אבל בקדשי בדק הבית מועלין בו ואמאן תרמייה דהא ודאי כרבי מאיר לא מיתוקמא דהא קא נסיב להלכתיה מלא לכם ולנו אלמא דאין עובדי כוכבים מקדישין לבדק הבית כלל וכר' יהודה מיהא לא אתיא דליכא לפרושי דלמסקנא משום רפיון ידים מיתוקמא שפיר כרבי מאיר דהא ליתא דרבי מאיר לא סבר האי טעמא דאם כן מנא ליה הלכתא דאין העובדי כוכבים מעריכין מקרא דלא לכם ולנו וצ"ע כיון דלרבי מאיר אין עובדי כוכבים מתנדבין לבדק הבית היכי תנן זה וזה מודים שנודרים הא עובדי כוכבים לא נודרין לבדק הבית לרבי מאיר ודוחק לפרש דנודרין קאמר למזבח דלכאורה מתני' דומיא דערכין דמיירי לבדק הבית ושמא טוב לפרש דרבא הדר ביה למסקנא זו מהא דאמר מעיקרא דהלכתא כרבי מאיר מקרא דלא לכם ולנו:
notes.en: If that is so, let one not be liable for misuse of it: according to Rabbi Yehuda. Why then is it taught, “But with consecrations for Temple maintenance one is liable for misuse”? To whom will you attribute it? It certainly cannot be established according to Rabbi Meir, since he takes his halakha from “You have nothing to do with us,” which shows that gentiles do not consecrate for Temple maintenance at all; and, at least [as Avimi explains him], it does not fit Rabbi Yehuda. Nor can one explain that according to the conclusion, that it is due to the weakening of hands, it fits Rabbi Meir well, for that is not so: Rabbi Meir does not hold this reason, for if so, from where would he derive the halakha that gentiles do not valuate, from the verse “You have nothing to do with us”? And it requires study: since according to Rabbi Meir gentiles do not donate to Temple maintenance, how did we learn [in the mishna], “Both agree that they vow”? According to Rabbi Meir, gentiles do not vow for Temple maintenance! And it is forced to explain that “they vow” refers to the altar, since the mishna apparently parallels valuations, which are for Temple maintenance. And perhaps it is good to explain that with this conclusion Rava retracted what he said at first, that the halakha follows Rabbi Meir because of the verse “You have nothing to do with us.”

notes.he: כיון דערכן נגנז לא ימעלו בו:
notes.en: If that is so: since their valuation is interred, one should not be liable for misuse of it.

messages.text: With regard to the five sin offerings that may not be sacrificed and are left to die, and similarly, with regard to consecrated money that is taken and cast into the Dead Sea, as it is not fit for any purpose, one may not derive benefit from them ab initio. But after the fact, if one derived benefit from them he is not liable for misuse, as the Temple treasury has no use for them.

notes.he: דהוו כחטאת שמתו בעליה דאזלא למיתה ואם נהנה אדם מהם אינו חייב קרבן דלא קרינא ביה מקדשי ה' (ויקרא ה) הואיל ולאיבוד אזלי:
notes.en: And money that goes to the Dead Sea: which is like a sin offering whose owner died, which is left to die; and if a person benefited from them he is not liable to bring an offering, since “from the sacred things of the Lord” (Leviticus 5:15) does not apply to it, as they go to destruction.

notes.he: אם נהנה מהן]:
notes.en: One may not derive benefit, and there is no liability for misuse: if one benefited from them.

messages.text: Why then is it taught in a baraita with regard to the consecrations of gentiles:

notes.dh: ואילו גבי קדשי עובדי כוכבים תניא
notes.he: בשחיטת קדשים בפ' ב"ש (זבחים מה:):
notes.en: Whereas regarding the consecrations of gentiles it is taught: in Sheḥitat Kodashim [Zevaḥim], in the chapter Beit Shammai (Zevaḥim 45b).

messages.text: In what case is this statement, that consecrations of gentiles are not subject to the halakhot of misuse, said? It is specifically with regard to consecrations for the altar. But with regard to consecrations for Temple maintenance, one who derives benefit from them is liable for misuse of consecrated property.

notes.he: דאין מועלין בקדשי עובדי כוכבים היינו בקדשי מזבח משום דגמרינן מעילה חטא חטא מתרומה מה תרומה אין מיתה נוהגת אלא בתרומת ישראל דבהדיא כתיב (ויקרא כ״ב:ט״ו) ולא יחללו את קדשי בני ישראל אף מעילה אינה נוהגת אלא בקדשי ישראל:
notes.en: In what case is this said: that misuse does not apply to the consecrations of gentiles — that is with items consecrated for the altar, since we derive misuse from teruma through “sin” and “sin” [a verbal analogy]: just as with teruma, death [at the hand of Heaven] applies only to the teruma of Jews, as it is written explicitly, “And they shall not profane the sacred things of the children of Israel” (Leviticus 22:15), so too misuse applies only to the consecrations of Jews.

notes.he: עובדי כוכבים של בדק הבית מועלין בהן. ומפרש התם מאי טעמא דכי גמרה מעילה חטא חטא מתרומה דומיא דתרומה דקדושת הגוף אבל קדושת דמים לא גמרינן מינה וטעם זה מצאתי מפורש בזבחים והוא עיקר שהרי בפירוש נשנה שם. ומפי המורה שמעתי בקדשי מזבח דעובדי כוכבים אין מועלין בהם משום דמצינו חילוק בין קדשי מזבח דעובדי כוכבים לקדשי מזבח דישראל שאין חייבין עליהן משום פיגול נותר וטמא כדאמרינן בשמעתא קמייתא דתמורה (דף ב:) אבל בקדשי בדק הבית דעובדי כוכבים לא מצינו חילוק הלכך מועלין בהן זה שמעתי וראשון עיקר. קתני מיהת מועלין בהן אלמא אינו נגנז מדשייכא ביה מעילה:
notes.en: But consecrations: of gentiles for Temple maintenance are subject to misuse. And it explains the reason there: when misuse is derived from teruma through “sin” and “sin,” it is like teruma, which has inherent sanctity; but sanctity of value we do not derive from it. I found this reason stated in Zevaḥim, and it is the main one, since it is taught there explicitly. And from my teacher I heard: items gentiles consecrated for the altar are not subject to misuse because we have found a distinction between gentiles’ altar consecrations and Jews’ altar consecrations, in that one is not liable for them for piggul, notar or impurity, as we say in the first passage of Temura (2b); but with gentiles’ consecrations for Temple maintenance we have found no distinction, and therefore they are subject to misuse. This I heard, but the first is the main one. In any case it teaches that they are subject to misuse; evidently it is not interred, since misuse applies to it.

notes.he: במסכת מעילה גבי קדשי עובדי כוכבים בד"א בקדשי מזבח דאין בהן מעילה אבל בקדשי בדק הבית מועלין בהן והני נמי אי נגנז כמעות ההולכות לים המלח דמי ולא ימעלו בהן:
notes.en: Why is it taught: in tractate Me’ila, about the consecrations of gentiles: In what case is this said? With altar consecrations, which are not subject to misuse; but with consecrations for Temple maintenance one is liable for misuse. And these too, if they are interred, are like money that goes to the Dead Sea, and one should not be liable for misuse of them.

messages.text: Why is this the halakha, given the fact that the consecrations of a gentile are interred?

Actually Rabbi Yehuda maintains that the valuation of a gentile is given to Temple maintenance and is not interred. And as for that which the Jews said to the gentiles in the time of the Second Temple: “You have nothing to do with us,” that refusal was not for halakhic reasons. Rather, it was due to the gentiles’ attempt to foster weakening of the hands of those rebuilding the Temple. As it is written: “Then the people of the land weakened the hands of the people of Judah, and harried them while they were building.”

verse.he: וַיְהִי עַם־הָאָרֶץ מְרַפִּים יְדֵי עַם־יְהוּדָה (ומבלהים) [וּמְבַהֲלִים] אוֹתָם לִבְנוֹת׃
verse.en: Thereupon the people of the land undermined the resolve of the people of Judah, and made them afraid to build.

notes.he: ודאי לבדק הבית אתי ובימי עזרא היינו טעמא דשלחו להם לא לכם ולנו:
notes.en: Rather, Rava said: it certainly goes to Temple maintenance; and in Ezra’s days, this was the reason they sent them, “You have nothing to do with us.”

notes.he: משום שלא היו מתכוונים לטובה אלא שיסמכו גם עליהם וישמעו לעצתם והם יאחרו הבנין עד שיסיבו את לב כורש שלא לבנותו:
notes.en: Due to weakening of the hands: because they did not intend good, but wanted [the Jews] to rely on them as well and listen to their advice, and they would delay the building until they turned Cyrus’s heart against building it.

notes.he: לעולם סבר ר' יהודה ערכן קדוש כשאר הקדש ויש בהן מעילה ומה טעם לא לכם ולנו לבנות משום רפיון ידים שמא אם יתנדבו הן וירצו לבנות עמהם יהיו מבטלין אותם שאין לבם לשמים כדכתיב ויהי עם הארץ [מרפים ידי עם יהודה] וגו':
notes.en: Rather, Rava said: Rabbi Yehuda actually holds that their valuation is sacred like other consecrated property and subject to misuse. And what is the reason for “You have nothing to do with us to build”? Due to the weakening of hands: lest, if they donate and want to build with them, they make them stop, since their heart was not for the sake of Heaven, as it is written, “Then the people of the land [weakened the hands of the people of Judah],” etc.

messages.text: The question of gentiles giving to the Temple continues on 6a, with two baraitot on whether a gentile’s pledge for Temple maintenance is accepted.
